utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-30-PT. The Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, good morning. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Keegan and Mr. Waidyaratne, for the Prosecution, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Krstan Simic, attorney at law from Banja Luka, for Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Zarko Nikolic, attorney at law, appearing for Milojica Kos, together with Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Toma Fila, attorney at law, with Mr. Zoran Jovanovic, Defence counsel for Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Simo Tosic, attorney at law from Banja Luka, and I appear for Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The purpose of this Status Conference is to review the progress. Of course, some progress has been made in relation to depositions, and I understand there will be a meeting concerning the depositions hearing after this hearing. And we welcome the progress which is being made and the work which has been done, I may say, on that particular topic. The matters which we have to deal with -- I should begin by saying, subject to this, there are, of course, only two of us sitting. Judge Robinson is absent for urgent personal reasons, as I hope everyone has been informed. That being so, normally, of course, motions are heard by three people, three judges, I should say. What we have in mind is hearing any argument. We shall, of course, not be able to make any decisions until we are fully constituted next Tuesday. But meanwhile we would propose hearing any oral submissions that anybody wants to make about the motions today, and we will deliver our orders when we are fully constituted after next Tuesday. If there is any objection to that course, would anybody state it now, and we'll hear any submissions. If there are no objections, we'll go along -- we'll go on to consider the various motions. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any Defence counsel want to make any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel also has no objections. No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into closed hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we back in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I said, dealing with depositions, Messrs. Radic and Kvocka have filed motions to add to their list, and Mr. Zigic has applied to vary his list. There's quite a number of witnesses it's sought to add. There is a withdrawal in one case. We have discussed this. It seems sensible, in fact, not to make any order on these particular motions at this stage, because the whole question of depositions is going to be considered after this hearing. And when you've heard what the presiding officer says, it may be that it will make a difference to the applications. So at this stage, we won't deal with those, unless there is anything somebody wants to say about them. Very well. The next matter is the issue of protective measures for deposition witnesses, and, well, it may be sensible to deal with those. As I understand it, there's no objection to our making orders for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, only in relation -- we filed a motion in relation to the motion that was filed on behalf of the defendant Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that in mind. I'll come to that next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But other than that, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll deal with these matters one by one, and perhaps if I could have a word with the legal officer, the presiding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In principle, we will make an order for protective measures. It may be that the presiding officer will be able to advise us as to precisely what's needed. But in principle, the order will be made. That brings us to the question of safe conduct, which Mr. Niemann mentions, and to that you've objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, our objection is not so much to the order ultimately being made in relation to safe conduct, provided that can be established, but on our reading of the material filed on behalf of the defendant Mr. Zigic, it occurs to us that, indeed, the statements would suggest the contrary; that is, that there's nothing contained in them that would suggest we would be seeking to indict them in any event, and therefore the order itself would not appear to be justified. That being the case, it's the position that we've taken is that these orders are of a serious nature and that if they are sought, they should be sought on the basis of the establishment of some prima facie need, and we submit that that hasn't been demonstrated. Secondly, Your Honours, our second objection relates to the request that there be constraints placed on the Prosecutor with respect to any subsequent indictment, and in our submission, Your Honours, the request for safe conduct has -- there's no necessity for that to go that far. The restraint is upon the Prosecutor in effecting arrest or indicting at the particular hearing. We accept -- provided there is a justification for it, we accept that is a reasonable constraint, and it's one which has been imposed upon us in other cases. We raise no objection to that, subject to the prima facie basis being established. But with respect to a constraint upon any subsequent indictment, we submit two things, Your Honours; firstly, that this accused has no standing to seek a constraint upon the Prosecutor's executive function in relation to indicting, on subsequent occasion, another person for whom they don't act. I mean a witness and an accused are different, and we submit, Your Honours, that in any event, that sort of intrusion on the role of the Prosecutor in filing an indictment is unjustified. Unless I can help Your Honours in any other matters, we rely on our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, in our experience, safe conducts are granted on occasion, but they are limited purely to the occasion of giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours, and we submit that that should be the basis of any order that Your Honours would seek to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, as we have done in the past. Very well. Thank you. We'll hear from the Defence on this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for the Defence in these constraints. In view of the status of the accused, and the status of the witnesses, on one occasion, as I mentioned on the previous Status Conference, Mile Ratkovic was supposed to be heard by one of the investigators, but he did not make a statement. In my absence, I didn't know what his status was, whether he was a suspect, a witness, and whether he was a witness for the Prosecution or witness for the Defence. I don't think that we are interfering with the rights of the Prosecutor, but, at any rate, when a witness makes a statement, the witness has to have certain obligations, in view of his own status. He should not be put in a position to be a suspect, if he is giving testimony anyway. I had this concrete example in the case of this Tribunal in relation to another one of my clients, who doesn't know whether he is going to be a witness in a certain case, and whether he is going to be a suspect with regard to another matter. So that is why I brought this up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider this and give a ruling in due course. The next matter concerns the disclosure of a videotape of an interview with the Prosecution by Mr. Kvocka and a number of photographs described as photo boards shown to Prosecution witnesses during questioning. Dealing with the photo boards first. As I understand it, the Prosecution have undertaken to disclose any photo board, or any relevant part of the photo board that will be used during the trial or which might contain any exculpatory material. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When are you going to do that, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the course of disclosure, Your Honour -- I mean, we intended to disclose additional material later on. Not a specific timetable; just a normal course of disclosure. Certainly well before the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to come back to disclosure at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To timetable it. Are you in a position, while you are on your feet, are you in a position to comply with a disclosure order fairly rapidly, if we were to make one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the next matter is the videotape of the accused's interview. Mr. Keegan, are you dealing with that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to Rule 66(A)(i), which provides for the disclosure of any prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the accused. Maybe there is no dispute about this, in which case it's unnecessary for me to refer to this Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is no dispute, but this is -- as I understand it, that relates to a statement by an accused to that accused. This request relates to a statement by another accused; in effect, a witness, if you will, a statement from a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Then let us find out the precise position. Who does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This is a request for the -- well, he asked for the videotapes of interviews of the other accused in this matter. He asked for the -- excuse me, the videotape -- the interview of Kos, and it's Mr. Kvocka's counsel who is making that request. So, in effect, we are dealing with a witness statement, if you will, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's not his own statement; it's the statement of a co-accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And our position merely is that this is treated as any other piece of potential evidence, as the Prosecutor determines that there is a basis for disclosure under the Rules. Either we intend to offer it into evidence or, pursuant to Rule 68, it needs to be disclosed to the Defence; we will do so. The tapes are in the -- are now being transcribed, and until such time as there is an official transcription of the videotape, it's an incomplete piece of evidence, if you will. And we are not in a position to make a final determination of its relative status vis-à-vis disclosure. As soon as we have a final transcript, and we make that determination, we will then disclose, if required under the Rules, or as we are obligated to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am thinking aloud. Normally, at least in a domestic jurisdiction, the accused would have access to statements to the police by their co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They do, Your Honour, except to the extent that that statement may contain information that is wholly unrelated to the particular case, and there may be requirements for protection of some or all of that information for other reasons. All I am simply saying is we are trying to treat this as we do any other piece of evidence, and we need an official transcription before we can be certain as to exactly what the contents of the videotape are and what portions, if any, or all, need to be disclosed. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the normal course of events, you would disclose it, unless there was material which for some reason or another you think should not be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. When are you going to deal with this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It's obviously a very lengthy transcript, Your Honour. It's in the process of being transcribed. I would anticipate it will be done within another two to three weeks. But, it's -- in the course of events, with all the other pressing matters for disclosure and translation, we are doing the best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, we'll hear the Defence about this. Clearly, it's a matter which should be resolved one way or another. We would have in mind to order disclosure within three weeks, or an indication of parts undisclosed, something along those lines, so that we get the matter into hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And in my discussions with Mr. Niemann, I mean, there was an intent to disclose it. It's simply a matter of waiting for the process. That was the only issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Mr. Simic, that's the order which we have in mind to make, unless you've got any submissions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept the arguments presented by my colleagues from the Prosecution; however, I raised this issue for the following reason: At the last Status Conference Mr. Fila opposed the disclosure of such documents. I got video recordings from the Prosecutor with Mr. Radic's statements, and I thought that this was the natural course to take. But in view of the objections taken by Mr. Radic's Defence, I believe, on the basis of Rule 68, the Defence is entitled to such evidence as well, and that is why we sent this request, so that the Prosecutor could give us all this evidence, which we consider to be essential and material, and this could also support Mr. Kvocka's Defence. So I accept this three-week deadline. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Kos's Defence also believes that the Defence attorneys for the other accused should be given such material. As far as the accused Mr. Kos is concerned, we don't think that there is anything that would be of a discreditory nature, and that is why we agreed to this. But may I mention, in passing now, that in that case the Defence of Mr. Kos is going to ask the Prosecutor to submit tapes with the statements of Mr. Radic, the accused Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Zoran Zigic's Defence presented a request to the Prosecutor for the disclosure of these materials in good time, so perhaps this was an omission made by the Prosecutor. We agree that this be submitted; and in good time, a month ago, we asked for this disclosure, just like Mr. Simic asked for Mr. Kvocka. So I don't want to go into all of that again. I don't think there is any need for us to submit a new request. I believe that there is no need for us to require this once again. And we also agree with what my colleague, Mr. Nikolic, Defence attorney for Mr. Kos, said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason why I opposed this last time is one that stands until the present day. It is not that the Defence attorneys for others should see what others have been saying. These tapes can be abused by it being released to the public, especially only certain segments, that something was said this way or that way. So what I think is that in the order it should be stated that the tapes may not be disclosed to anyone else. That is the only thing I asked for. I think this is only natural. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for the record, we did of course respond to the request from Mr. Tosic, and informed him, in essence, the same way we responded to this motion, that we were in the process of getting the videotapes transcribed. And if there was discloseable material pursuant to our obligations, we would disclose it. That's certainly our intent. It's just a question of the resources. These are particularly difficult to transcribe, based on the nature of the interview and the quality of the equipment. And we obviously agree to the protective measures, although I think they would be covered by the existing orders in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will make any order subject to particular protective measures in this case. So that's probably right, that the broad order covers it. But we will specifically identify these items as not to be disclosed, as indeed they should not be. The final matter, as far as motions are concerned, is a motion on behalf of Mr. Kvocka for his provisional release. As I said earlier, this is not a matter which we can deal with or make any order in respect of in the absence of Judge Robinson. We can hear any oral submissions that anybody wants to make, if that's agreeable. Bear in mind, of course, that we have the written submissions already. But, Mr. Simic, if there is anything you would like to add, we would, of course, hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I agree for my submission to be heard today and for the decision to be made when the Trial Chamber is complete. As is usually, we submitted a motion explaining our position, requesting the application of Rule 65 and for the provisional release of Mr. Kvocka, for him to defend himself from freedom. We will not go through all the reasons which we have cited in our submission, but we would like to point to some particular facts that we consider important. Having in mind such a sensitive question as this, which has already been discussed before the International Tribunal, the concept of criminal law resides on the presumption of innocence, that a person is innocent until proved guilty. And this is also accepted in the Statute of the Tribunal, according to Rule 21(3). Based on this concept, many points are then developed as far as overall criminal law is concerned, and, of course, an important issue in this respect is the issue of detention. Of course, we will all agree that in the concept of modern criminal law, it is accepted that detention is an exceptional matter because it affects the most subtle aspects of a person's freedom, his relations to his family, restrictions on his movement. So detention is a measure which could be applied exceptionally, but the general rule is that people are free to move freely, to perform the functions that they are supposed to perform by nature and society, until the time that they are pronounced guilty and sentenced. The question of detention before the Tribunal was also discussed at a round table which was organised in November in 1998 in Belgrade, and it was organised by the Fund for Humanitarian Rights. It was attended by experts on this matter, including Ambassador Scheffer from the United States, who was representing the U.S. government on issues of war crimes. Unfortunately, Madame Arbour, then the Prosecutor, and President McDonald were unable to attend at that time because the Yugoslav authorities did not issue them visas in order to enter the FRY. It would have been very beneficial if the President and the Prosecutor had been able to attend. But this is a very delicate legal issue, there is no doubt about that, and one of the conclusions was the Tribunal will receive a proposal to review all of these issues and consider, to date, practice and also its own regulations where detention is imposed as obligatory, as an obligation, detention which, in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, is contrary to the concept which has been adopted in modern criminal law, that detention is an exceptional measure and is only imposed in exceptional circumstances. Of course, we have in mind that the work of the International Tribunal is specific. It has a different concept of law. But this concept of law cannot be contrary to all of the ideas which are prevalent in modern criminal law today. The accused are accused of serious crimes, but we are also aware, as practice has shown, that there are people with varying degrees of responsibility, and we can see that this is reflected in different sentences passed by the Tribunal, as the sentences show for Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Jelisic, who was sentenced to 40 years. So we are aware that each Trial Chamber can decide whether a person can be trusted, whether they have enough responsibility, in light of the fact that every person is innocent until proved guilty. And for that reason, I believe that this question should be opened up before the Tribunal in the spirit of the ideas prevalent in contemporary law and, of course, without prejudice to the fact that the persons who are before you here, and others who will be before you here, have been accused of serious crimes but, nevertheless, they are people. The institute of detention has two main elements which we need to review. The first is the guarantee that the accused will appear before the Trial Chamber. So we have to create a secure mechanism and system that the accused will not use his release in order to unable proceedings to continue or prevent the carrying out of justice. The second question which we need to consider is whether the accused, by being released, if he is granted this confidence by the Trial Chamber, will influence or tamper with witnesses, and having in mind the nature of this case, these would mostly be victims. So we need to consider these two questions regarding Mr. Kvocka, and we need to stick to concrete facts. I had a meeting with Mr. Blewett, the Deputy Prosecutor, yesterday, and we reached a high degree of agreement, accord, on these questions, especially concerning the fact that the political and social situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina is still quite complex and that it was essential to open up true processes of cooperation which are, first of all, in the interests of justice, on one side, and also in the interests of the accused, because these processes of cooperation will create possibilities for the carrying out of justice. But also there will be a possibility, for people who are in this position, to exercise more easily their right to defence, easier access for them to documents, or for them to have a more substantial logical support. We also agreed that the results have not been great in this aspect, and I will not deny this here today. But I do have to say, in order for you to understand this issue about the results, that a person has to be well informed about the circumstances in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska. The government is facing a particular problem as far as the implementation of the Dayton Accords is concerned, and this is a question that concerns cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. So all political options are viewed in the light of cooperation with the Tribunal as an institution which needs to ensure a lasting and stable peace in the region and, in a certain way, so that in the future we would avoid conflicts like this. All the indictments and all the publicly-indicted persons have been -- the Republika Srpska has been informed about that, but all of the people sitting here have never received those indictments. They were never handed to them, because up until 1998 there was an obstruction of everything that came from the Tribunal and everything that had anything to do -- any connection with the Tribunal. This is true, and I substantiate these claims with an interview by Mr. Kvocka. Mr. Kvocka, several days before his arrest, gave an interview to Mr. Chris Bennett, a person who is the deputy of the director of the International Crisis Group. This interview was published in the news Slobodna Bosna. This magazine is published in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A day earlier, Mr. Kvocka gave a public interview to Channel 5 of British Television. He gave this openly in his front yard, where it was taped, and he literally said that he never received an indictment, that no one had ever informed -- gave him any information regarding this, and everything that he knows, he knows from the media, from the press. And as he said, everybody already knew about this; this was public knowledge. Mr. Kvocka also said clearly and concisely that he was not afraid, that he was moving freely throughout Prijedor, that he was passing by members of SFOR, and he was even afraid that because of that statement of his, members of SFOR would have problems, because they were not arresting him even though there was a warrant issued, and that he absolutely had no intention of running; he had no intention of running away. He confirmed this just three days after the publication of that interview. Mr. Kvocka was arrested then. He is one of the few people who were arrested in a dignified manner, without any use of force, because simply his interview seemed to be an invitation for the arrest. And that is why we believe that the Trial Chamber should, to a sufficient degree, appreciate the specific circumstances, and that is that Mr. Kvocka was not arrested, nor that he had any information about that, and that he had no intention to run, which he indicated before he was arrested. This is the question that we need to discuss. The second question: There are specific relationships in the Republika Srpska. If Mr. Kvocka had received the indictment, in view of the attitude towards the Tribunal, the satirisation of the Tribunal and denial of its existence, and having in mind that his wife is a Bosniak, and because of the security of his family, Mr. Kvocka was not in a position to turn himself in, and we are not hiding that. Even if Mr. Kvocka had been handed the indictment and had he waited, Mr. Kvocka was in his house, waiting to be arrested, because during any kind of arrest, tensions are raised, political tensions, and this is very difficult to explain. I think this fact also needs to be taken into account. Another question which concerns the status of detention is the effect on victims. I have to say that the indictment and also the evidence disclosed by the Prosecution does not place Mr. Kvocka in any situation in which he personally undertook any act which could have elements of a war crime in relation to any particular person. He never insulted anybody. He never hurt anybody. What's more, according to the information from the indictment in accordance with Rule 18 of the Statute, Mr. Kvocka was not even present in a situation without reacting, if there had been any incidents. So in such a situation, there is no fear that Mr. Kvocka could influence anybody, anybody, regarding their testimony or the execution or the carrying out of justice. Mr. Kvocka is a police officer, a person who, in his class, was among the top ten students, a person who, as an exceptional police officer, was chosen to provide security to the Yugoslav embassy in France by the former Yugoslav. He worked there for two years, and he showed some exceptional work then. He performed the same job -- he was supposed to perform the same job in Rio de Janeiro, but for family reasons, he was not able to go. So I appeal to the Trial Chamber, in making its decision and in considering the objective criteria, to take into account also the situation in Republika Srpska, which is very difficult to explain and difficult to understand, difficult to describe. It is difficult to explain what happened in '92 and '91. We will need time to understand that. I must point out that the government of Republika Srpska has issued guarantees, and in issuing these guarantees the government of Republika Srpska set out from -- it checked the past and the professional career and the record of Mr. Kvocka. His two sisters are married to Bosniaks; they still are to this day. One of them is a victim of this civil war and is a refugee now. His wife's family have also become refugees, so Mr. Kvocka really is in a specific situation. His family in Banja Luka is under serious pressure. And in the facts that you have probably become familiar with, you are aware of the status of mixed marriages. And we have a document of uncontested facts from the Prosecutor, asking us to accept that mixed marriage was the biggest heresy at that time. And of course what went on at that time will be something that we discuss during the case itself. So I don't need to go into any details about that now. I would like to add that in the meantime Mr. Kvocka's wife is ill. She has some form of cancer. So now she's undergoing medical treatment. She's quite afraid. And I believe that provisional release of Mr. Kvocka would be -- constitute major support to his wife, who has had to bear a heavy burden during the civil war. I know that this, in principle, is not a reason which needs to be taken into consideration in particular, but in view of the overall situation, I hope that some special understanding will be shown for that. I have been working with Mr. Kvocka for the past two years, as his Defence attorney. The Defence is ready to accept other orders. It is also prepared to submit bail for the provisional release. If the Trial Chamber should request additional guarantees, we are prepared to accept this, because we really believe that Kvocka has an interest to appear before the Trial Chamber in order to fight -- in order to prove his innocence. He believes he is innocent, and the most important thing to him is to prove that innocence. He does not intend to run away. He said as much before his arrest. And Mr. Kvocka also has no place to run. His wife is unemployed. He's here. He has two children. It has been said that he is suspected of war crimes, so Mr. Kvocka, even if he did have such an intention, has absolutely no place to run. And he does not have any intention of running. Due to the above, I believe that a decision on provisional release would be socially responsible, from the aspect of opening up the process that I talked about, the process of cooperation between the Tribunal and institutions of Republika Srpska. I would also like to inform you that at this moment the activities are being undertaken to adopt such a law. In the assembly, we would like to adopt a law which would regulate relations between institutions of Republika Srpska and the International Tribunal. If we should succeed in adopting such a law, we would create what we have said, and that is cooperation between the Court and institutions -- government institutions of Republika Srpska, as well as protected citizens. So such a decision, a favourable decision, would be a good contribution in order for this process to receive the force that it should have. We really need to have confidence and trust in people. This is a Tribunal for war crimes, and the persons before you have been accused for war crimes, and there will be more such persons who are still to be accused. We are aware of that. But simply this trust and confidence has to be mutual. In talks which I had, there is always the question of the first step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I don't want to interrupt you, but I think you've had about 20 minutes. Anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just wish to add that I expect, in view of the complexity of the situation, I think that it would be very useful for the first step to be made by the Tribunal. And, believe me, the results of such a first step would become evident very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, we have your response, which we have just received. Is there anything you want to add to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just briefly, in light of the submissions this morning. I certainly won't repeat our submission. Of course, the starting point here is that there is a confirmed indictment; that is, an accepted prima facie case of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law committed by this accused. And, of course, the length of detention is not in and of itself determinative of the issue. So we get to the standards to be applied. As indicated in the brief, while we would certainly welcome a change in the law on cooperation in Republika Srpska, the fact is that the law of that entity still states that they will not turn over anyone to this Tribunal. And the actions heretofore of that entity should speak louder than the representations of what hopefully may be a change in policy. And we would welcome that. But that being the case, if in fact it appears that Republika Srpska would not turn over this person, based on past behaviour, and the current state of their law, it would leave it to the accused to somehow deliver himself before this Tribunal, if he were to be provisionally released. And I note the statements of counsel, that the accused could not turn himself in earlier on the basis of the indictment, due to the potential pressure on his family. We would suggest there is certainly nothing to indicate that that pressure would be any different now, should he be released, and it perhaps would be even greater, thereby preventing him from returning on his own. So it is in fact the circumstances that all the evidence indicates, that neither the government nor this accused would be willing to ensure his return before this Tribunal, if he were to be released. With respect to the threat of others, we have certainly briefed that fully in our response. We believe that nothing in the submissions indicate any different, other than that the release of this individual would raise the significant potential of threat to witnesses and victims, either by the accused himself, or by others who might be involved by his release and, in an effort to prevent him from having to return, attempt to influence or threaten witnesses. Once those two issues are determined, and they are the two most important issues, the question of potential threat to others and, of course, the indications of his willingness or ability to return for a trial, there is also, of course, the impact that such a provisional release would have on others, including international institutions, the public in general, and victims and witnesses in other cases. And we believe, once those first two criteria are reviewed, this additional criteria is also important for consideration. The Prosecution position is that he should not be granted provisional release. And unless I can assist you with any further issues, Your Honour, those would be my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. We'll consider this matter in due course, and give our judgement. Mr. Simic, you've taken up a lot of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two sentences, please. It is quite understandable that detention can be ordered only in a prima facie case, that is to say, the Rules certainly took that as a point of departure, that is to say, to order detention against persons whose indictments were confirmed. When I talked about pressures with regard to Mr. Kvocka turning himself in, I talked about '97 and the beginning of '98. The circumstances have changed considerably now, and I would like the Trial Chamber to take that into account in view of what the Prosecutor said. That's all I wish to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. As I say, we will consider these matters and deliver our judgement in due course. Mr. Niemann, I am going to deal next with the progress of the case. Clearly, some progress has been made, but the fact remains that these accused have been in detention for nearly two years, and that is a matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And one which must be addressed in terms, if possible, of getting the trial on. Now, the position of the Trial Chamber is this: that we are engaged on a trial in another case, which began in the spring of last year, and is likely to go on for most of this year. That said, it is necessary to consider starting other cases, and that we propose to do. We are not in a position today to say when this case will start, or in what order we will start other cases, but what we want to be in a position to do is, if necessary, to be in a position to start it in as short a time as possible. So, to start with, how much notice would you require of a trial date? Normally, of course, at a Status Conference you fix a trial date and it's way in advance, and everybody can work to it. But we are not in that position at the moment because of the uncertainty of our work. But it might assist to know how quickly we could get this case on, if the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the most convenient period for us to get this particular trial started would be a 30-day period. That would give us time to inform our witnesses that we are about to start and get the matter ready for trial within 30 days of receiving notice. If that's considered too long, Your Honour, we could discuss the possibility of what endeavours we could put in place to do it shorter than that. But if that was a period considered acceptable to the Tribunal, that is a period that would certainly be convenient to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that seems a reasonable period to ask for, considering the work that has got to go into it in getting the matter ready. On that topic, perhaps I should turn to the Defence and ask you what time period. Could you work to a 30-day notice of a trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of all the Defence counsel, I wish to say that 30 days is fine with us. We know that the Prosecutor had problems with the witnesses and, after all, we are talking about events from 1992, and now is the year 2000, so this is a reasonable deadline. However, with your permission, Your Honour, I would like to propose something at this point in time, if Mr. Niemann and his co-workers agree, something that would speed up the proceedings even more. We agreed, as you know, that we start with depositions, and in this way the Defence would have very little evidence to be presented at the trial itself, 5 or 10 witnesses per accused or per Defence attorney, which really is not too much. However, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity, having consulted my colleagues, Krstan Simic and Zarko Nikolic, to propose something to you which would speed up the proceedings even more and, perhaps, reduce the number of witnesses the Prosecutor has to bring before this Honourable Trial Chamber. And that is to say, to have the trial start by the accused, Kvocka and Radic and Kos, start by making their own statements. So we could start that way, and perhaps then the Prosecutor would need less evidence than otherwise. I am familiar with the statement made by the Honourable Judge Rodrigues, and that is to say that a lot of time was wasted in General Blaskic's trial, and this became obvious only at the very end. We don't want this Trial Chamber to be in the same position; that is to say, that at the very end of the trial, the Trial Chamber realises that a lot of time has been wasted for something that is not contested. So if the Trial Chamber agrees, and if the Prosecutor agrees, we could start with the three I mentioned. Mr. Zigic's situation is different. If he wishes to testify, he can testify, but he doesn't have to. But this is different. And he really has nothing to do with the organisation of the camp, as the others would speak about. Thank you. I have thus concluded my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would draw your attention, Mr. Fila, to a fairly new Rule, 84 bis, which, in fact, I think probably caters for what you have in mind. And it doesn't require anybody to consent to it, but allows the accused to make a statement at that stage. You might want to have a look at it and avail yourself of that Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a look at it, Your Honour, and that is why I made this proposal. This concerns an entire testimony, a complete testimony, as we do at the very end. This new Rule is not very clear, what it actually envisages. Is it only one statement. I suggest that an entire testimony be heard, not a mere statement; an entire testimony. That's the difference. And that is why I need your agreement, as well as that of Mr. Niemann. Because if somebody gives this kind of testimony, then there is no cross-examination. And this implies cross-examination. So that could really expedite the proceedings, and speed up the trial itself, whereas their regular statements, their ordinary statements, so to speak, you can see on the tapes, those that were made by the policemen at the prison in Scheveningen. So that's a one-sided thing. That's the difference. Thank you for your remarks, but, yes, I did bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the problem about the suggestion, and we'll certainly consider it and it may be possible, but again, without looking into it, I think that the Rules of Procedure lay down a time for the taking of evidence, starting with the Prosecution and then going on to the Defence. Now, it may be that we could work another solution, but I don't know. Thank you for the suggestion. Let's not debate it now. We will consider it as to what can be done. If I could turn to the Prosecution now. If 30 days were the time of notice of trial, what seems to be outstanding before the case is ready is the question of disclosure, and I'm just turning to you to see how rapidly, Mr. Niemann, that could be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the only issue that's of concern to us about disclosure is the matter that my colleague Mr. Keegan discussed concerning the translation issue. As far as I'm aware, Your Honour, there are some translation materials which are still awaited. If we were confronted with a proposal to have the matter set down for trial, we would go to the appropriate translation people and see whether or not it could be accomplished. If we had any difficulty in doing that, we would come back to Your Honours on that. At the moment, because there is no date, as such, it's difficult for us to argue any specific urgency in relation to the nature of the work that's being undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But provided we can be assured that matters of disclosure are being pursued, as it were, apart from that is there any reason why you shouldn't disclose everything else? You may have done. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's absolutely no reason why anything that we have in our possession shouldn't be disclosed. The only matters that I understand are delayed are those which await translation. And I intended this as no criticism of the translation unit, You Honour, and I must add that. As I understand it, there's nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a great deal of work for them to do, as we know. Can I then turn to the more general aspect of the case, and that is the size of the case. We note with concern that in March of last year we were told that the Prosecution case would involve about 60 witnesses, with a time estimate of eight weeks. In June, that had grown to 80 witnesses, and I don't think we were given a time estimate. But working on the basis which I remember Mr. Niemann mentioned on about the first day I ever sat in this Tribunal, each witness seems to take about a day, each Prosecution witness. Unhappily, events over the last two years have confirmed that, in my experience, that we're not moving much faster than that, although it may be possible in some cases to do so. But that being so, we have to look at this case in comparison with other cases. This case is in a fairly short time frame and in a fairly short compass as far as place is concerned. It's one place, or there are several places but one locality, and within a relatively short two-to-three-months time frame. Now, compared with other cases in this Tribunal, that is a relatively short compass, and we have been discussing this matter and have come to the conclusion that we must ask the Prosecution, if not require them, to reduce the scope of their case. Now, I recognise that that's not always an easy task, but we have to look at the other cases that we have to try, the fact that there are not only these accused in the detention unit; there are others who are facing trial by this Chamber. I've told you the position as far as the Trial Chamber's work is concerned. Given all those considerations, we think that this case should be completed, as far as the Prosecution are concerned, in eight weeks, as originally envisaged, with about 60 witnesses. Now, to this end we propose to set another conference which will be conducted by the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Bennouna. We have looked at our calendar, and the only time which we can identify is Tuesday, the 15th of February, between 4.30 and 6.00. I'm sorry it has to be so late, but the fact is that we have another case to try and that must go on that day. But if we finish that, as we normally do, at 4.00, then a hearing can take place, as far as this case is concerned, at 4.30. It is proposed that the Judge, the Pre-Trial Judge, will go through the statements which are being disclosed by the Prosecution, with a view to reducing the number of witnesses and reducing the scope of the case. So the Prosecution should be prepared for that exercise in three weeks. Now, we will hear any submissions, of course, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, naturally we would like to reflect upon what Your Honour said before we say or have any concluded view on this. At the outset, I think it's important for us to emphasise that we are anxious to ensure that the case is reduced to the absolute minimum that we can achieve in any event. Your Honours, we agree entirely that the time frame of the crimes that are alleged and the geographical focus is limited, but we would submit that the allegations contain a very significant number of events which we would argue are part and parcel of the presentation of this Prosecution, and with the mechanisms that we have available to us, we can only best achieve this by calling witnesses. Initially, we had rather optimistically hoped that we could avail ourselves more of the deposition process. We appreciate and understand the position of the Defence, and we realise that they have particular interests in Your Honours observing Prosecution witnesses and their demeanour first-hand, which limited the number of witnesses we could call by this process. We will do what we can to cooperate in every way to achieve the objective that Your Honour set. The only issue that I raise, though, Your Honours, is that if Your Honours were to indicate an eight-week period, if that was what was concluded as to be the maximum reasonable time that can be available to us, we would ask that we not be restricted by the number of witnesses so much but by the time, because there are means by which we can at least approach the Defence to see whether some of the issues that can be resolved by way of statements or whatever can be covered, thus shortening the length of testimony of witnesses. So it may be that we can get much more readily or rapidly to the kernel of the evidence, not necessarily by reducing number of witnesses but by reducing the length of their testimony in chief and in cross-examination. But unless I can assist Your Honours with other matters, that's our position at this stage, and certainly we'll be in a position to address all these matters on the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. I think that we need to consider your proposal, and it can be of great help to the Chamber, to try the case within a reasonable period of time, to limit the length of statements, of testimonies, keeping in mind that affidavits can corroborate statements that have been given here or testimonies that have been given here before the Trial Chamber. Then we could limit the testimonies to what is absolutely essential, and to new elements only, and to what can confirm -- to confirm what has already been said, then we can use affidavits and documents such as these. We keep in mind that you said that you want to get in contact with the Defence in a spirit of cooperation. That's the spirit of cooperation that has been shown by Mr. Fila, when he said that he wants the trial to be as fair and as speedy and efficient as possible. I think we can work in that spirit. Now, I would like to invite you to think of the proposal that was put forward by Mr. Fila earlier on. You don't have to answer right away. He said that maybe at the beginning of the trial, we could hear the testimonies of Kvocka, Radic and Kos. If I understood correctly, Mr. Fila wants to go beyond Rule 84 bis, and we would like you to think about it. You don't have to give us an answer straight away, but maybe we could talk about it again during the hearing of the 15th of February at 4.30 p.m. As far as I'm concerned, I'm going to study very carefully the summaries that you have handed over. I'm going to study them. I think they are, indeed, very useful because they are very detailed, and I'm going to study them in order to see in what way we can be as rational as possible as far as the witnesses are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honour, we will certainly consider very carefully what Mr. Fila has suggested, and we will follow up with him on any issues of clarification as to precisely what he proposes. It's been my experience in other cases that Mr. Fila has been very cooperative with this Tribunal in endeavouring to reduce the length of the trials, and I feel some confidence that in discussions that I may have with him, that we could have some success in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could I perhaps add this: that, of course, the shorter the trial is anticipated to be, the easier it is for the Trial Chamber to accommodate it within its calendar, if that is an incentive to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's certainly an incentive to the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we deal with questions of review of detention under Rule 65 bis, which we are required to do, are there any other matters which any party wants to raise? If there are no other matters, I will formally ask if anybody, including the accused, wants to raise any matters in relation to issues of detention. Anybody want to say anything? Yes, Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ZIGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Regarding detention, I don't have anything to say, even though I do have some slight difficulties there. But I would like to talk about some materials that I have in possession in my room. On several occasions, we received from the Prosecution translations of witnesses -- I'm sorry, I apologise. Your Honour, I would like to -- you mentioned numbers of 60 to 80 witnesses. In my room, the information says 186. Out of those 186, I only have 90. So the Prosecution has not given me 88 translations of statements, and here we are discussing the start of trial. And it's a very big job for me to look at completely new witness statements, 88 of them, and I have still not received that. So I would need a lot of time to read that, because I would like to participate in my own case as much as possible. Further, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber if this is possible. It doesn't have to be an order or a written instruction to the Prosecution, but I am confused about materials that relate to witness statements. The statements I have, the majority of them are marked in three different ways, so a witness is referred to as Witness 10, but then in other material he's referred to as Number 20, and then in something else again he's referred to as Number 50. So I am completely confused, and I am sure that the Prosecution must be confused too, because they have the same witness. There is a lot of confusion here. We really cannot find our way through all of that. And this is not only our problem, the problem of Defence, but I believe of the Prosecution too. So is it possible for the Prosecution to introduce some kind of order, so if there are 186 witnesses, as we have been informed, to mark them from 1 to 186 so that we have a definite indication, so that if Witness 57 appears tomorrow, we know that this is Witness 57 and that this witness will not be referred to by some other number? Thank you, Your Honour. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zigic. Well, that seems to me to be a matter which can be sorted out between the Prosecution providing a witness list and also the Defence, so that the accused is not confused as to which witness is which. Perhaps, Mr. Keegan, you could have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We'll adjourn this matter. There is a meeting as to depositions, and Judge Bennouna will sit on the 15th of February for the next hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.52 a.m., sine die. 25
